summary: Koken Sasaki was a scholar of Buddhist studies and Sinology who studied at Rissho University (~1950–1960). He spent his career at Rissho University, serving as associate professor (~1970–1977), department head (~1977–2002), professor/director (~1995–2002), and professor emeritus (~2002–2008).
Koki Kawagishi was a Buddhist studies scholar who held posts as professor at both Eizan Gakuin and Shitennoji University, as attested in 1976.
Konchok Drakpa studied under Patrul Rinpoche and Jamgon Ju Mipham Gyatso. He was a teacher of Dilgo Khyentse Rinpoche.
Konchok Gyatso is a Tibetology scholar who studied under Sherab Gyatso. He held an attested post at the Tibet Academy of Social Sciences in 2014.
Konchok Zangpo pursued studies under both Patrul Rinpoche and Jamgon Ju Mipham Gyatso.

Konrad Klaus specializes in Indology and Tibetology. He studied at the University of Göttingen and the University of Marburg under Michael Hahn, later serving as Vertretungsprofessor at Bochum, Marburg, and Bonn (1999–2001) before succeeding Claus Vogel in 2001.

Kosaku Hamada worked in history, archaeology, Sinology, and Japanology. After studying at the University of Tokyo (~1901–1904), he held positions at the University of Tokyo (~1905–1909) and Kyoto University (~1909–1938).

Kosei Ishii specializes in Buddhist studies and philosophy. He studied at Waseda University under Akira Hirakawa, earning his doctorate in 1994, and held positions at Waseda, Komazawa Junior College (1994–2006), and Komazawa University (professor of Buddhism, 2006–2021).

Kosei Tada was a Buddhist studies scholar who studied at the University of Tokyo (~1961–1967). He held a post at Taisho University (~1970–2009) and served as director of the Society for Buddhist Cultural Studies (attested 2004).
Koshin Suzuki is an Indology and Buddhist studies scholar who completed doctoral studies at Taisho University, where he also held a post as a researcher (attested 1995–1998).

Koshiro Tamaki worked in Buddhist studies, Indology, and philosophy. He studied at the Fifth Higher School and the University of Tokyo, later serving at Toyo University (1954), the University of Tokyo (1964–1976), Tohoku University (~1976–1979), and Nihon University (1979–1986).

Kosho Kawamura, a Buddhist studies and Indology scholar, studied at Toyo University under Giyu Nishi, Nichijin Sakamoto, Shunkyo Katsumata, Koshiro Tamaki, and Yoshiro Tamura. He worked at Toyo University (~1957–1995) and held posts at Minobusan University and Nava Nalanda Mahavihara.

Kosho Mizutani studied Buddhist studies at Ryukoku University (~1952–1956) and Bukkyo University (doctorate, 1979). He served as associate professor (~1962–1973) and president (~1979–1989) at Bukkyo University, and later led Tokai Gakuen and Bukkyo Kyoiku Gakuen (~1999–2011).

Kosho Uchiyama worked in Buddhist studies and philosophy, studying Western philosophy at Waseda University (~1934–1937) and under Kodo Sawaki (1941). He taught at Miyazaki Catholic Seminary (~1937–1941) and succeeded Sawaki as abbot of Antai-ji (1965–1975).

Koshu Itabashi was a scholar of Buddhist studies who was educated at Sendai Daiichi High School, the Imperial Japanese Naval Academy, and Tohoku University (~1949–1953), where he studied under Teruji Ishizu.

Kosuke Nakazawa is a Buddhist studies scholar who served as professor (attested 2001) and professor emeritus (attested 2026) at Rissho University, and held a post at the Institute for the Comprehensive Study of the Lotus Sutra (attested 2001).

Kotatsu Fujita was a Buddhist studies and Indology scholar who studied at Tokyo and Harvard. He taught as associate professor at Osaka University (~1962–1968), professor at Hokkaido University (~1968–1979), and former president of Sapporo Otani Junior College (1992).
Kotetsu Yoshida is a Buddhist studies scholar who served as professor emeritus at Taisho University and advisor at the Kawasaki Daishi Research Institute, both attested in 2014.
Koun Kajiyoshi was a scholar of Buddhist studies who studied at the University of Tokyo (~1928–1931) and held a post at Taisho University from around 1940 to 1975.

Koun Yamada worked in Buddhist and religious studies. Educated at the First Higher School, he studied under teachers including Hakuun Ryoko Yasutani, whom he succeeded (1961–1989), and founded the Kamakura Haku-un-kai in 1953.
